**Tafsir (commentary) on Surah al-Ma'idah**

**Commentary on the Tafsir of Surah al-Ma'idah.** The Shaykh, the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Surah al-Ma'idah is entirely Madani, except for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion﴾. It was revealed at 'Arafat, as we will explain. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: all of it is muhkam (definitive, unabrogated); none of it has been abrogated (naskh, the abrogation of a ruling by a later revelation). Al-Sha'bi said: none of it has been abrogated, except the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾, as we will explain.

It is narrated from Abu Maysarah that he said: Allah the Exalted revealed in this Surah eighteen rulings that He did not reveal in the rest of the Qur'an.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾. We have already mentioned that everything in the Qur'an that begins with "O you who believe" was revealed in Madinah, and everything that begins with "O people" was revealed in Makkah. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: When you hear Allah the Exalted say "O you who believe," give it your full attention, for it is either good that you are commanded to do, or evil that you are forbidden from.

As for His saying: ﴿fulfil the contracts﴾. It is said that "awfa" and "wafa" have the same meaning. As for "al-'Uqud" (the contracts): 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah al-Walibi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: By "al-'Uqud" He meant what Allah has made lawful and unlawful, and what He has obligated and set as limits.

Mujahid said: By "al-'Uqud" He meant the covenants (al-'uhud). It is also said that the difference between 'aqd (contract) and 'ahd (covenant) is this: 'ahd is the command concerning a thing, and it is said: "I charged so-and-so with such-and-such" (ʿahidtu ila fulan kadha), meaning I commanded him with it. 'Aqd is a command together with firm binding. The contracts include vows, and all binding contracts, which must be fulfilled, except an oath to do something permissible, which need not be fulfilled, according to the Sunnah, which is what is related from the Messenger of Allah that he said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else to be better than it, let him expiate his oath and do what is better."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle﴾. Al-Hasan said: By it He meant camels, cows and sheep. Qutrub related from Yunus: they are camels, cows, sheep, horses and barbary horses. Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Beasts of cattle" are the wild cows, wild donkeys and wild gazelles. The beast (bahimah) was called bahimah because of the ambiguity (istibham) in it, since it has no speech that can be understood; and for this reason it is also called 'ajma' (dumb).

The intended meaning of "beasts of cattle" is the cattle themselves, but it was idafah (annexed) to itself, as one says "the soul of the human" (nafs al-insan), "the truth of certainty" (haqq al-yaqin), and similar expressions. Qabus ibn Abi Zabyan related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Beasts of cattle" are the unborn young (al-ajinnah).

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾, meaning what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ ﴿...not hunting while you are in the state of ihram (sacred state)﴾. It is said that it is in the accusative as an exception (istithna'), and it is said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "not making lawful the hunting." Just as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿not waiting for its ripening﴾, meaning, not waiting for its ripening, ﴿while you are in ihram﴾, in which is the prohibition of hunting during the state of ihram. ﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "The sha'a'ir (rites) are the marked offerings (al-hada'ya al-mushaarra), that is, those marked by ish'ar (marking). They used to prick something on the hump of the camel until it was smeared with blood, and that is the ish'ar of the offering (ish'ar al-hadi), and it is a sunnah." Mujahid said: "By the sha'a'ir he meant the rites of Allah, and not the sacred month, nor the offering, nor the garlands, nor those coming to the Sacred House seeking..." meaning the rites (mashaa'ir) of the Haram, such as al-Safa and al-Marwa and others. The intended meaning is the prohibition of killing within the Haram.

﴿Nor the sacred month﴾. Ikrimah said: "He meant by it Dhu al-Qa'da." Others said: "Rajab." It was also said: "It is an expression for all the sacred months." His saying: ﴿nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾. Al-hady is the plural of hadiyya, and by it is meant the camels of the offering. As for al-qala'id, these are the camels that are garlanded, and they used to garland the camels of the offering. 'Ata' said: "He meant by it the owners of the garlands, for it was the custom of the people of the Haram to garland themselves and their camels with some bark of the trees of the Haram when they wished to leave, so that they would not be molested. So the Law forbade interfering with these things."

﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾, that is: do not molest those intending the Sacred House. The occasion of revelation of this was what is reported: "Al-Hutam ibn Dsubay'a came with a group of people to the Messenger of Allah in Madina, and he offered them Islam, but they did not accept and made excuses and departed, until he (peace be upon him) said concerning him: 'He came with the face of an unbeliever and departed with the back of a treacherous one.'

He went off and drove away the livestock of Madina, and they pursued him but did not catch him, while he was driving the camels and chanting:

(The night has wrapped him in a driver, Hutam... He is neither a shepherd of camels nor of sheep,)

(Nor a butcher upon the back of a Wadm...)

When it was after the conquest of Makka, the Muslims met him during the pilgrimage season, as he was going on pilgrimage, and with him were camels of his people and garlands. They set out for him, and the Prophet met him, pointed to his companions and said: 'Take the man!' so that they would seize him. Then the verse was revealed forbidding interference with him and with his rites and garlands." Al-Sha'bi said: "This was ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾, and ﴿when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾, and ﴿let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, incite you to transgress﴾, and ﴿cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ likewise. Then it was abrogated by His saying: 'Kill the polytheists.'"

His saying: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: "He meant by it the bounty of trade." It was also said: it is the reward. ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. This is a command of permission; it permitted hunting for that state.

﴿Nor let the hatred of a people incite you﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Jarm" means "to earn," and it is said: "So-and-so jarama his family," that is, earned for his family. And he recited:

(Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyayna a blow that earned Fazara, after it, that they should be angry.)

That is, earned. Al-A'mash recited: ﴿wa la yajrimannakum﴾ with a damma on the yā', and it is sound in Arabic; it is said: "jaruma" and "ajrama," with one meaning. It was also said: its meaning is: "Nor let the hatred of a people incite you," that is, the enmity of a people.

﴿Because they barred you﴾, that is, because they barred you. Abu 'Amr recited "in ṣaddūkum" (if they barred you) as a conditional, and the meaning of the verse is: let not the enmity of a people who barred you ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾ incite you ﴿to transgress﴾ against them.

(And cooperate in righteousness and piety.) Al-birr: truthfulness. It was also said: al-birr is abstaining from every forbidden thing. There is another view: al-birr is Islam, and al-taqwa is the Sunnah.

﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression.﴾ Al-ithm: disbelief; al-'udwan: innovation. It was also said: al-ithm is disbelief, and al-'udwan is injustice. ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are dead animals, blood﴾. As for "dead animals" (al-maytah), it is any animal that has died; and "blood" is the blood of an animal that is spilled and poured out, which is prohibited. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) used to put the blood into intestines, cook them, and then eat them. So the Sharia (shari'ah, the divine law) came with its prohibition. Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the spleen, and he said, "Eat it." It was said to him, "Is it not blood?" He said, "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, has only prohibited poured-out blood."

﴿And the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: meaning, that over whose slaughter the name of other than Allah has been pronounced. It was also said that it is what is slaughtered for idols. So these four are prohibited. It was also said that these were permitted in some earlier law, to the point that it is said that Adam, peace be upon him, descended to the earth with the prohibition of these four.

﴿And the strangled animal﴾ is the sheep that is choked with a rope so that it dies. ﴿And the beaten animal﴾ is the one that they used to beat at the idol until, when it died, they ate it. (And the fallen animal) is the one that falls from a high place and dies.

﴿And the animal killed by the goring of another﴾ is the one that another animal gores so that it dies. ﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾ is also read with the ba' vowelled with a sukun for lightness, and its meaning is "what remains of what the beast of prey has eaten." ﴿Except what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾: He prohibited these kinds and excepted the one that has been properly slaughtered. The root of tadhkiyah is "completion." It is said: "dhakkaytu al-nar" when I completed its kindling; and it is said: "fulan dhakiyy" when he has complete understanding. The zakah in the Sharia is well known.

﴿And what is sacrificed on the altar stones (nusub)﴾: meaning, on the idols. The nusub is a type of idol. The difference between them and idols (asnam) is that idols are the figures that are carved and painted, while the nusub are neither carved nor painted. It was also said that they had stones set up around the Ka'bah, which they worshipped, drawing near to them with sacrifices and smearing them with blood; so the Sharia prohibited it.

﴿And that you seek to divide by arrows (al-azlam). That is a transgression.﴾ Al-istiqsam is seeking one's share. Al-azlam are the arrows (aqdah), singular "zalam"; it is also said "zulm" or "zalm," and they are arrows that were kept by the custodians of the Ka'bah. On one was written "Go forth," on another "Do not go forth," on one "My Lord has commanded me," and on another "My Lord has forbidden me." There was also one blank, called "mutanih," with nothing written on it. ﴿By the arrows; that is a transgression. Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me. Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favour upon you, and I have approved for you Islam as a religion. So whoever is compelled...﴾ A man among them, when he intended to travel, would come to the custodian of the House and have the arrows shuffled; if the blank came out, he would shuffle them again until another came out. If what was written "Go forth" came out, he would go out on the journey; and if "Do not go forth" came out, he would not go out. The Sharia forbade this. Among such things are judgement by the stars, casting pebbles (darb al-hasa), omens (tiyarah), and soothsaying (kahanah), and all of these are forbidden. He said: "Whoever practises augury, or has it done for him, or practises divination, will not look upon Paradise on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Sha'bi and others said: the arrows were for the Arabs, and the knucklebones (ka'ab) for the non-Arabs.

As for His saying: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them but fear Me﴾: this is because the disbelievers used to hope that the Muslims would return to their religion, until Mecca was conquered and Allah made Islam manifest; then they despaired of that. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾, that it would vanish, and that they would return to their religion.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾: this was revealed at 'Arafat while the Messenger of Allah was on his she-camel al-'Adba'; she knelt down from the weight of the revelation. It is narrated that a Jew said to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "You recite a verse which, had it been revealed to us, we would have taken the day it was revealed as a feast," meaning the day on which it was revealed. 'Umar said: "I know on what day it was revealed and where: it was revealed on Friday evening at 'Arafat," and he indicated that this day is a feast for us.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ is: in the laws and rulings, because it was revealed after the laws and rulings had become settled. It was also said: no ruling was revealed after this verse, so much so that it is said that His saying ﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾ in the verse on kalalah was revealed before this verse, and it was also said after it.

Know that the laws were not revealed all at once, but gradually, piece by piece. At the beginning, when he was in Mecca, the obligation was to utter the two testimonies, to believe in the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell, two rak'ahs in the morning and two in the evening, and to restrain their hands from fighting and to be patient over the harm of the polytheists. Then, on the night of the Mi'raj, which was eighteen months before the Hijrah, Allah enjoined upon him and his community fifty prayers, then it was reduced to five prayers, as is known in the account. Then, when he emigrated to Medina, Allah enjoined upon him jihad and zakah; then fasting in the third year after the Hijrah, and the Hajj in the seventh year after the Hijrah. Then the conquest of Mecca. Then, at the Farewell Pilgrimage, this verse was revealed in the tenth year after the Hijrah, and no ruling was revealed after it, as we have explained. The Messenger of Allah lived eighty-one nights after that and died on the second day of Rabi' al-Awwal. It was also said that he died on the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, and this is more sound.

His emigration was also on the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, and he completed ten years, and departed from this world.

There is another view: that the meaning of His saying ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ is: I have made you secure from the enemy, I have made your religion manifest, I have completed My favour upon you, and I have approved Islam as a religion for you. 'A'ishah narrated from the Prophet that he said: "Allah, Exalted is He, says: I looked into the religions and chose Islam as a religion for you; so honour it with generosity and good character as long as you keep company with it, for the miser is far from Allah, far from people, far from Paradise, and near to the Fire."

﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger﴾: al-makhmasah is the emptiness of the belly from food; and in the proverb: "Fullness is followed by emptiness." ﴿Without inclining toward sin﴾: meaning, not inclined to sin, which is exceeding satiety in eating carrion, or eating it for pleasure. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them.﴾ The occasion of revelation of the verse: Zayd ibn al-Khayl al-Ta'i and 'Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i asked the Messenger of Allah and said: "We hunt with dogs, so what is lawful from it [the game] and what is unlawful from it?" Then the verse was revealed. It is also said: the occasion of revelation of the verse was that the Prophet, when Allah commanded the killing of dogs, [the verse ﴿Allah has taught you, so eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it, and fear Allah; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ was revealed], and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us from this community which has been commanded to kill them?" Then the verse was revealed. The first is more sound.

﴿Say: The good things have been made lawful for you.﴾ "The good things" are everything that the Arabs find pleasant and enjoy, provided that no Book or Sunnah has declared it unlawful. ﴿And what you have taught of the hunting animals⦅al-jawarih⦆﴾, i.e., the predators that seize prey. It is said: jaraha and ijtaraha, meaning he earned/acquired. From this the hand is called jariha (a limb that acquires), because it acquires. The poet said:

(She with a fine, graceful brand, who recalls the hunting animal, and what was earned [jarh])

i.e., what was acquired. ﴿Trained (mukallibin)⦅trained hunting animals⦆﴾. In the irregular readings it was recited "mukallibin." It is said: kallabahu, so he is mukallib, and aklaba, so he is mukallib, when his dogs multiply, and this is like their saying amsha when his livestock increase. The poet said:

(Every youth, even if he has many herds and wealth, the vicissitudes of the world will snatch him away.)

Al-Azhari said: the meaning of the statement is: "and lawful for you is what you have taught of the hunting animals, at the time of your training them and making them eager for the hunt." Know that the permissibility of game is not restricted to hunting by dogs, according to the view of the majority of scholars.

Tawus said: it is restricted to it, holding to His saying ﴿trained﴾, but this is an anomalous opinion. The meaning of His saying ﴿trained﴾ is: urging and inciting [the animals] to the hunt, and all hunting animals are alike in this. ﴿You teach them from what Allah has taught you⦅you train them in what Allah has taught you⦆﴾.

﴿So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it.⦅Allah's name⦆﴾ He permitted the hunting of hunting animals when they hold it for the owner, and there is no disagreement about this. As for when they eat from the game, is it still considered held for the owner, and is it lawful? There is disagreement among the Companions about this. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Salman al-Farisi said: it is lawful, to the point that Sa'd said: "Eat whatever your dog seizes, even if a piece of it remains [jadiyya, i.e., a piece]." This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Adi ibn Hatim said: it is not lawful, and this is al-Shafi'i's second opinion, and most exegetes held this view. As for the discussion of the basmala (saying the name of Allah), it will come in al-An'am. ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾. Mentioning "today" here is superfluous (ṣila). We have already explained the meaning of "the good things" (al-ṭayyibāt). There is also another view: that "the good things" means the pure things, and everything pure is lawful.

﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾. Mujāhid and Ibrāhīm al-Nakha'ī said: by this is meant the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book. ﴿And your food is lawful for them.﴾ If someone asks: how is our food made lawful for them, and how is this prescribed for them, when they are disbelievers and are not people of the Law? al-Zajjāj answered: its meaning is: it is lawful for you to feed them. So the address of permissibility is directed to the Muslims. Another scholar said: He said this because right after it He mentioned the ruling on women (ḥukm al-nisā'), and did not mention the permissibility of Muslim women for them. So it is as if He said: it is lawful for you to feed them, and unlawful for you to marry them.

﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women﴾. This refers back to the first structure and is separate from His saying: ﴿And your food is lawful for them.﴾ ﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾. al-Ḥasan said: by this is meant the chaste (al-'afā'if). Mujāhid said: by this is meant the free women (al-ḥarā'ir). From this comes the permission of a free People of the Book woman for a Muslim man, and the implication of the prohibition of a People of the Book slave woman. This is the view of most scholars, and it is the view of the scholars of Kufa such as al-Sha'bī, al-Nakha'ī, Sa'īd ibn Jubayr and a group. This applies to the protected (dhimmiyya) People of the Book woman. As for a free People of the Book woman who is a combatant (ḥarbiyya), according to the view of most scholars she is lawful for a Muslim. Ibn 'Abbās said: she is not lawful. It was recited as ﴿al-muḥṣanāt﴾ with a kasra on the ṣād. The chastity (iḥṣān) of a People of the Book woman is that she abstains from fornication (zinā) and performs the ritual bath from impurity (janāba). ﴿When you have given them their wages (ujūrahunna)﴾, that is, their dowries (mahūrahunna), ﴿being chaste, not committing fornication, and not taking secret lovers﴾.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deed has become void﴾. Mujāhid said: by this is meant: whoever disbelieves in God in whom he believes. al-Kalbī said: by this is meant: whoever disbelieves in the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahāda). al-Rabī' ibn Anas said: by this is meant: whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an. al-Zajjāj said: the meaning of His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾ is: by making the forbidden lawful and the lawful forbidden, that is, whoever deems the forbidden lawful or makes the lawful forbidden, ﴿his deed has become void.﴾ This is closer to the arrangement of the verse concerning permissions and the making lawful of prohibited things. His saying ﴿his deed has become void﴾ means: his deed has been nullified. ﴿And he, in the Hereafter, is among the losers.﴾

The word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to [perform] the prayer﴾ means: when you intend to rise to the prayer. This is like His words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning: when you intend to recite. You say: "If you trade, then trade in goodness," and "If you sit with someone, then sit with so-and-so," meaning: if you intend to sit with him.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that wudu' (ablution) be obligatory at every rising to prayer. However, through the Sunnah we know that it is permissible to combine prayers with one wudu'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) combined four prayers on the day of the Trench with one wudu', and he combined five prayers on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to the prayer, then wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾ [applies] with one wudu'. It is related from Ali (رضي الله عنه) that he said: "Wudu' is for every obligatory prayer." It has also been said: it is recommended. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the implied wording of the verse is: when you rise to the prayer from your beds (al-madaji'), meaning from sleep. Then the obligation of wudu' is due to the state of ritual impurity (hadath), because sleep is a state of impurity.

﴿So wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows﴾, meaning: together with the elbows. Al-Mubarrad said: when a thing is extended up to its own kind, the limit (al-ghayah) is included in it; when it is extended up to something other than its kind, the limit is not included in it. So His words ﴿up to the elbows﴾ extend up to its own kind, and therefore the limit is included in it.

As for His words ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, it extends up to something other than its kind, so the limit is not included in it. The word al-mirfaq (elbow) is so named because a person leans on it (yartafiq) by resting on it.

﴿And wipe over your heads and your feet up to the ankles﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with the accusative (naṣb) [on the basis of coordination with the washed members]; so its implied meaning is: "wash your faces and your hands and your feet." The rest read ﴿wa-arjulikum﴾ with the genitive (kasr).

The scholars differed concerning the obligation of washing the feet. The majority of scholars, and the consensus (ijma') today is upon it, hold that washing the feet is obligatory. It is related from Ali that he said: wiping over the feet is permissible, and this is what is obligatory; and a difference of opinion from him is also related. Al-Sha'bi said: the Qur'an was revealed with two washings and two wipings. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: one may choose between wiping and washing, due to the difference in the recitations.

The more correct view is that washing is obligatory, and the Sunnah indicates this. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "[...] and if you are in a state of janabah (major impurity), then purify yourselves; and if you are [...]" "Woe to the heels from the Fire." It is also related in a marfu' report: "Allah, the Exalted, does not accept the prayer of any one of you until he places the purification (tuhur) in its proper places: he washes his face, then his hands, then wipes his head, then washes his two feet."

He also said: "No man performs wudu', washes his face, except that his sins that he looked at with his eyes are expelled with the water or with the last drop of water [...] and when he washes his feet, his sins that his feet walked to are expelled with the water or with the last drop of water." And it is related that he saw a man who had performed wudu' and a part of his foot the size of a fingernail had not been touched by water; so he said: "Go back and perform the wudu' well." His ordering him to go back is evidence of obligation.

As for His words ﴿and your feet up to the ankles﴾: whoever reads with the accusative, it is clear regarding the obligation of washing. As for whoever reads with the genitive, its implied meaning is: "wipe your heads, and wash your feet." It is permissible for one thing to be conjoined to another even if it differs from it in the action. The poet said:

"And I saw your wife in the battle, / girding a sword and a spear."

Meaning: girding a sword, and carrying a spear on his back. Another said:

"I fed them chaff and cool water."

Meaning: and I gave them cool water to drink. So likewise His words ﴿wipe your heads and your feet﴾ mean: "wash your feet"; except that it is in the genitive by way of following (al-ittiba') and adjacency (al-mujawarah), as the Arabs said: "the hole of a worn-out lizard (juhr dabb kharib)."

Abu Zayd al-Ansari, who is an imam of the language, said: the Arabs sometimes call a light washing "masḥ" (wiping). The Arabs say: "Tamasah, O so-and-so," meaning: "perform ghusl." So conjoining it with wiping does not negate washing. Therefore it is permissible that the intended "wiping" on the head is literal wiping, and on the feet it is washing; and because washing the feet, for the most part, does not lack some wiping, it is permissible to call their washing "wiping." His words ﴿up to the ankles﴾ mean: together with the ankles, as we explained regarding the elbows. Al-Ka'bān (the ankles) are the two bones protruding on either side of the foot.

﴿And if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves﴾, meaning: perform ghusl. ﴿And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself (al-ghā'it), or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth (ṣa'īdan ṭayyiban) [for tayammum]﴾, and we have already explained the discussion of this. ﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾. His words "with it" (minhu) are evidence that ṣa'īd is earth (turab), since wiping with it is established.

﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship﴾, meaning: any constriction. ﴿But He intends to purify you and to complete His favor upon you that you may be grateful﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: by completing the favor is meant the expiation of sins through wudu', as we have related; and this is like His words: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier sins and your later ones, and complete His favor upon you﴾, meaning: by forgiving the sin. In wudu' there is expiation of the sins one committed in this world, and a light on the Day of Resurrection. He said: "My community will come on the Day of Resurrection with radiant marks (gurr muhajjalun) from the traces of wudu'; so whoever among you is able to prolong his radiance, let him do so."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you﴾. Mujahid said: He meant by it the covenant which Allah, the Exalted, took from the offspring of Adam before the creation came into being. And Ibn ʿAbbas said: He meant by it the covenant which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took from everyone who embraced Islam, to hear and obey in ease and hardship, in what is pleasing and what is disliked. ﴿When you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. That is: of what is in the breasts.

Almighty Allah says: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice﴾. That is: be persistently standing firm in justice, speaking the truth. ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verses 9–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness﴾. It has been said that this is in the accusative position (manṣūb), and the verb of promise (wa'd) falls upon it. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

(I saw the righteous, for them is a reward... and gardens, and a spring called Salsabil.)

Others said: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ is the beginning of a statement, meaning: for them is forgiveness that has been promised, and its place is in the nominative position (marfūʿ): ﴿for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jaḥīm).

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verses 9–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness﴾. It has been said that this is in the accusative position (manṣūb), and the verb of promise (wa'd) falls upon it. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

(I saw the righteous, for them is a reward... and gardens, and a spring called Salsabil.)

Others said: ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ is the beginning of a statement, meaning: for them is forgiveness that has been promised, and its place is in the nominative position (marfūʿ): ﴿for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jaḥīm).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ Al-Hamm (al-hamm, "resolve"): the soul's inner discourse toward an act. It is said: "ahamma bi-sh-shay'" and "ihtamma bihi," meaning he was concerned with it or intended it, when he gave it his attention.

Regarding the occasion of revelation of the verse there are two accounts. Jabir said: its cause was that "the Messenger of Allah was on some journey, and his companions scattered among the acacia trees in a resting place. The Messenger of Allah dismounted beneath one of them and hung his sword upon it. A Bedouin came, drew his sword, stood over his head, and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'Allah, exalted is He.' So his sword fell from his hand and he went away, and the verse was revealed."

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and a group said: the verse was revealed for another cause, namely: "The Prophet had a covenant between himself and the Banu Qurayzah that they would assist him, and he would seek their help against the polytheists. One day he came to them seeking their help regarding the blood-money of the two men of 'Amir (and he dismounted) beneath a wall. They resolved to kill him by treachery, and one of them, who was called 'Amr ibn Hajjash, said: 'I will drop a stone upon him, so that you may be rid of him.' Then Jibril descended and informed him of that." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah had certainly taken a covenant from the Children of Israel, and We appointed from among them twelve leaders (naqib)﴾. The naqib (leader) of a people is like the ra'is (chief). Abu 'Ubayda said: the naqib is the kafil (guarantor). Someone else said: he is the amin (trustworthy one). The naqib is above the arif (overseer), and the munkab is an assistant to the arif. He was called naqib because of the searching and investigation that he carries out.

﴿Allah took the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We appointed from among them twelve leaders. And Allah said, "Indeed, I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakat, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that..."﴾

The story concerning this is that Musa, upon him be blessings from Allah, appointed over his people twelve naqibs, one naqib over each tribe (sibt). It is narrated that he sent them to the city of the giants (al-Jabbarin) to find out and gather information about their condition. When they returned, they frightened the Children of Israel from fighting them, and said: "You cannot withstand them." They opposed the command of Musa, except for two men among them: one of them was Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun), and the other was Kalib ibn Yuqanna (Caleb son of Jephunneh). Their story will come explained in full.

﴿And Allah said﴾, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, I am with you﴾, meaning: with victory. ﴿If you establish prayer, give zakat, believe in My messengers, and support them﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is "honour them" (ta'zim). Someone else said: "assist them" (nasr). Ta'zir in the language means discipline (ta'dib), and the root meaning of ta'zir is prevention (man'); for this reason discipline is called ta'zir, because it prevents the one being disciplined from doing what he was disciplined for. It is narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "The Banu Asad have begun to discipline me (ta'zirunī) regarding Islam," meaning: they are disciplining me.

﴿And loan Allah a goodly loan﴾, which is the giving of zakat. Zayd ibn Aslam said: its meaning is spending on one's family. It is narrated from one of the early Muslims (salaf) that he heard a man say: ﴿Who is it that will loan Allah a goodly loan?﴾ Whereupon he said: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest."

﴿I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that [among you] has certainly strayed from the even way﴾, meaning: he has erred from the path of truth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant We cursed them⦆ "Ma" here is redundant (ṣila), meaning: "for their breaking" (fa-bi-naqdihim) ﴿their covenant, We cursed them﴾, that is, We removed them far from mercy. ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, that is, dry and not soft, such that mercy does not enter them. It is also read "qasiyya" (qasiyah). It was said: its meaning is "qāsiya," with the form fa'īl in the sense of fā'il (active). It was also said: its meaning is that their hearts were not purely of faith; they lived between disbelief and hypocrisy. From this comes "al-darāhim al-qasiyya" (the qasiyya dirhams), which are the adulterated ones. The poet said: (Its neighings in the hard horses' hooves ... are like the ringing of the qasiyya coins in the palm of the money-changer.)

He likened the neighing of the horses on hard stones to the sound of dirhams in the palm of the money-changer (al-ṣayrafī). ﴿They distort words from their places﴾. Their distorting of words is their altering of the description of the Messenger. It was also said that what is meant by it is their distortion through bad interpretation. ﴿And they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾, that is, they forgot a share of what they were reminded of. Ḥaẓẓ (portion) means naṣīb (share).

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾. It was said: al-khā'ina is al-khiyāna (treachery), a fā'il used in the sense of a maṣdar, like al-qā'ila in the sense of al-qayūla (afternoon rest). This is the saying of Qatada. Mujahid said: its meaning is "a treacherous group" (firqa khā'ina), because the verse concerns the Jews; this interpretation is consistent. ﴿And you will not cease to discover﴾ according to His saying: ﴿treachery from them﴾ ﴿except a few of them﴾, meaning: those who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and a group.

﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾, that is, turn away from them and do not confront them. It was also said: this was abrogated (mansūkh) as well by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God﴾ in Surat al-Tawba ﴿Indeed, God loves the doers of good﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from those who said, "We are Christians"﴾ — and from the Jews. The correct view is that the verse refers specifically to the Christians, because the Jews have already been mentioned. Al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "In this there is evidence that they are called Christians by their own naming, not by the naming of Allah, may He be exalted." ﴿We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾ — this is as we explained regarding the Jews. ﴿So We incited﴾, that is, We caused to fall, ﴿among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Al-ighra' (incitement) originally means adhesion, and from it comes al-ghara' (glue). Its meaning is: We made enmity cling to them until they became sects and factions, among them the Ya'qubiyya, the Malkaniyya, and the Nestoriyya. ﴿And Allah will inform them of what they used to do.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book﴾. What is meant by it is the People of the two Books: the Torah (al-Tawrah) and the Gospel (al-Injil). However, He mentioned "the Book," which is a generic noun (ism al-jins), so it applies to both groups. ﴿There has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal﴾ from the Book. That refers to those who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning (ayat al-rajm), and the like. ﴿And he pardons much﴾ means: he overlooks much of what they concealed, so he does not raise it.

﴿There has come to you from Allah a light﴾. It has been said: it is Islam, and it was called a light because one is guided by it just as one is guided by light. It has also been said that it is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was called a light because things are made clear by him just as they are made clear by light. ﴿And a clear Book﴾ is the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah guides by it those who pursue His good pleasure to the ways of peace﴾. That is: Allah guides by it, to the ways of peace, those who pursue His good pleasure. Al-Suddi said: "al-Salam" is Allah, exalted is He, and "subul al-salam" (the ways of peace) is the path of Allah, exalted is He. And he said: "al-Salam" is "al-salamah" (safety, freedom from harm), like "al-lidhadh" and "al-ladhdhah" having one meaning; and what is meant by it is the paths of safety.

﴿And brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾. That is: from disbelief (kufr) to (Islam). Disbelief is called darkness because one is bewildered in darkness, and Islam is called light for the reason we have explained. ﴿And guides them to a straight path﴾. It was said: it is Islam, and it was said: it is the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 17:

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ It was said: this is the statement of the Ya'qubiyyah (Jacobites) among the Christians, who said: indeed the Messiah is God. And it was said: when they said "the Messiah is the son of Allah," the son of every person is of his own kind, so it was as though they said: the Messiah is Allah.

﴿Say, "Then who could prevent Allah at all if He intended to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?"﴾ That is: who is able to repel the command of Allah? ( ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is competent over all things.﴾ ) In this is an indication that the one deserving of divinity is the one to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens, and who has this power; so it is Him alone that you should worship.

The Exalted said: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of God and His beloved."﴾ It means: God is to us like a father in tenderness and affection, and we are like children in closeness and standing.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said, concerning the Jews: They found in the Torah, "O children of my rabbis (aḥbārī)," so they altered it and read, "O children of my firstborn (abkārī)." From this they said, "We are the children of God and His beloved."

As for the Christians, they related about Jesus that he said, "I go to my Father and your Father." From this they said, "We are the children of God."

﴿Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾ It means: a father does not punish his son, and a beloved does not punish his beloved. That is, why would God punish you for your sins, if He is, by your claim, your Father and your Beloved? Then He said: ﴿Rather, you are mortals of those He has created.﴾ That is, you are human beings among the created beings. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and to Him is the final return.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after a interval [of no messengers]﴾. That is, after a cessation of messengers. They differed concerning the time of the fatra (interval). Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: The time of the fatra was between 'Isa and Muhammad, and it was six hundred years. It was also said five hundred years. He named it the time of the fatra because the messengers came after Musa in succession without interruption, whereas after 'Isa there was no messenger except Muhammad. ﴿Lest you should say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner."﴾ The Kufans said: its meaning is: "lest you say." The Basrans said: its meaning is: "out of aversion that you should say," and this is like the two views concerning His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾, and ﴿There has certainly come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and Allah is over all things competent﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He made among you prophets"﴾, meaning: from among you prophets. ﴿And made you kings﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, possessors of servants and retinue. Qatadah said: No one before them had servants and retinue, so when they had servants, they became kings. Mujahid said: its meaning is: no one enters upon you except with your permission, and whoever no one enters upon except with his permission is a king. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever among the Children of Israel had a servant, a wife, and a mount, was a king." It is also narrated that a man came to 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and said: "I am one of the poor among the Emigrants." He said: "Do you have a dwelling to which you retreat?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a wife with whom you find tranquility?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You are among the wealthy." The man said: "And I have a servant who serves me." He said: "You are among the kings."

As for al-Suddi, regarding the earlier scholars, its meaning is: "and made you kings" meaning you control your own affairs, and He freed you from the enslavement of Pharaoh. Al-Mu'arrij said: He meant by it: "and made you good people," and "al-muluk" (the kings) means "the good" in the dialect of Hudhayl and Kinanah.

﴿And gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds﴾, meaning: the manna and the quails, the bursting of the stone, the shading of the clouds, and the like.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which God has ordained for you﴾. It was said: it is Damascus, Palestine and part of the Jordan. Qatadah said: it is all of al-Sham (Greater Syria). It was also said: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and the land of Tur (Sinai).

And His saying ﴿which God has ordained for you﴾ means: God has granted it to you (wahaba). It was also said: God has decreed (fard) for you that you enter it. ﴿And do not turn back on your heels, for then you will turn about as losers﴾.

"Their words, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, 'O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants (jabbarin).'﴾ Al-jabbar (the one who compels): it is every oppressor who forces people to his will. Allah, exalted is He, is al-Jabbar, who compels His creation to His will, and this is from Him truth and deserving of praise. As for jabarut (tyranny/arrogance) for creatures, it is blameworthy. The root meaning of jabbar is the one who magnifies himself and refuses to be humbled or subdued. From this it is said, 'a jabbara palm tree' when it is tall and out of reach of hands. Those people were called jabbarin because of their height and because they resisted through the strength of their bodies. The story concerning this is that these people were in the city of Ariha (Jericho) in al-Sham, and in it were a thousand villages, in each village a thousand orchards. In it were the 'Amaliqah (Amalekites) and a remnant of the people of 'Ad, and it is the city of the jabbarin.

'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that Moses (peace be upon him) had sent those chieftains, who were twelve chiefs (naqib), to that city in order to learn about their condition. When they arrived there, a man from among them met them, took them all together in his sleeve, brought them to the king, and scattered them before him, and said, 'These are the ones who came to fight us.' The king said, 'Return and inform them of what you encountered,' and they returned.

In some tafsir works it is mentioned that they took a cluster of grapes and placed it on a pole between two men until they were able to carry it, and they took two pomegranates and loaded them on a beast that could barely bear them. When they returned to the Children of Israel, they frightened them and said, 'You will not be able to withstand them except for two men from among them: Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yuqanna,' and He mentioned both of them in the other verse. As for the rest of the Children of Israel, they opposed and refused to fight them, and said, 'O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants. ﴿And we will never enter it until they leave it; so if they leave it, then we will enter.﴾'"

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Two men from among those who feared, upon whom Allah had bestowed His favour, said﴾. They were Yusha' and Kaleb. (They) said: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate, for when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious﴾. That was a gate which they knew that, if they entered through it, they would prevail.

(And it is read) in the irregular readings: "Qala rajulani min alladhina yukhafuna" with the yā' vowelled with a ḍammah (yukhāfūna), so its meaning would be: two men from those Amalekites. It was said: two men of them became Muslims, and they said this statement: ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are within it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ And this is well known. Al-Hasan said: "They disbelieved by this statement." Others said: "Rather, they committed fisq (transgression) by opposing His command." The interpretation of His saying, ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾, meaning: "So go, you, and let your Lord help you in the fighting." There is another view regarding it: that the meaning of His saying, ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾, is: "and your kabir (greater one, elder)," and they meant his elder brother Harun. The Arabs call the greater one rabb (lord). Allah, exalted is He, said in the story of Yusuf: ﴿Indeed, he is my rabb; he has made my residence excellent﴾, meaning: "my kabir," and by it he meant "the Aziz of Egypt." It is possible that they said that to Musa out of ignorance and dullness, and so they committed fisq by it. Ibn Mas'ud narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he went out on the day of Badr, al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr said to him: "We will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Musa: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting right here,﴾ but rather we say: 'Proceed wherever you wish, [for] we are proceeding with you.'" It is also narrated that the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you were to drive your mounts to Bark al-Ghimad, we would journey with you." That is, to drive the camels' livers (akbad al-ibil) to Bark al-Ghimad, which is a place.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have no authority except over myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ Its meaning: I have no authority except over myself, and my brother has no authority except over himself. It was also said its meaning is: no one obeys me except myself, and no one obeys me except my brother. ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾ means: separate us. And it was said its meaning is: judge between us and the defiantly disobedient people.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said: "Then it shall be forbidden to them"﴾. It has been said that the speech ends here, and its meaning is: the holy land is forbidden to them forever. He did not intend by it a prohibition of worship (tahrim ta'abbud), but He intended a prohibition of barring (tahrim man'), for they were barred from it, so they never entered it, and only their children entered it. It has also been said that the verse is connected, part to part.

They were forbidden it for forty years, as He said: ﴿It shall be forbidden to them for forty years﴾.

(They wander in the land.) God, may He be exalted, had confined them to the wilderness (al-tih) as a punishment for what they had opposed. It has been said: the wilderness (ard al-tih) in which the Children of Israel wandered was six farsakhs in length and twelve farsakhs in breadth, and the number of those who wandered in it was six hundred thousand. They would stand in it, and whenever they set out in the evening from a place to travel, they would find themselves in the morning at that same place; and whenever they set out in the morning from a place to travel, they would find themselves in the evening at that same place. So it went on every day until they died in it. It has also been said: Musa and Harun were among them, and both died in the wilderness. It has also been said: they were not among them, and that this was only a punishment upon them. When they died in the wilderness and their children grew up, Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) set out with their children toward the holy land, fought the Amalekites, and God, may He be exalted, gave him victory over them until he conquered that city. It was a Friday, and the day grew tight for them, so God, may He be exalted, held back the sun for an hour until he conquered the city; then the sun set on the night of Saturday, since it was not permissible for them to do any work on the Sabbath. God struck fear into their hearts on Friday. This is the summary of the discussion concerning His saying: (﴿for forty years they shall wander in the land﴾, so do not grieve), that is, do not be sorrowful ﴿over the defiant people﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 27:

The Most High's words: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth, when they each offered a sacrifice﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid said: He means by it two sons of Adam from his own loins, Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain). Al-Hasan said: He means by it two men from the Children of Israel. The more correct view is the first.

As for the story concerning this: it is said that Hawwa' (Eve) would give birth to a boy and a girl with each pregnancy. She bore a pair, Habil and his sister, and bore a pair, Qabil and his sister. So God the Most High commanded Adam to marry Habil's sister to Qabil and Qabil's sister to Habil. But Qabil was not pleased and said: "I have more right to my sister," for she was more beautiful than Habil's sister. In some of the exegetical works it is related that Qabil said: "I have more right to my sister, because I am of the offspring of Paradise, and Habil is of the offspring of the earth." It is also said that Hawwa' conceived him in Paradise, and for this reason he said: "I am of the offspring of Paradise." So Adam commanded them both to offer a sacrifice, and whichever of them had his sacrifice accepted would be more entitled to that sister.

Habil was a owner of sheep, and Qabil was a farmer. Habil deliberately chose a ram from the best of his flock, and Qabil deliberately chose the worst of his crops. They placed them in a spot, and fire came and consumed the sacrifice of Habil, and that was the sign of acceptance at that time, while it did not consume the sacrifice of Qabil. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿when one of them was accepted and the other was not accepted﴾, meaning Habil was accepted and Qabil was not. ﴿He said: "I will surely kill you."﴾ Qabil envied him and intended to kill him. Habil answered and said: ﴿"Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous."﴾, meaning those who refrain from sins.

It is related from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "If I knew that Allah the Most High had accepted one prayer of mine, it would be dearer to me than this world and all that is in it, because Allah the Most High says: ﴿Indeed, Allah accepts only from the righteous.﴾" Qatadah said: The righteous (al-muttaqun) are the people of "There is no god but Allah."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you; indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: It was [part of the law of Adam that] whoever intends to kill another, it is obligatory upon the one targeted to refrain from defending himself and to endure the harm, and this was also the case in the law of our Prophet (ﷺ) at the beginning. As for His saying, ﴿I shall not stretch my hand toward you﴾, it means: in defense. It has also been said: that was not a law, but he said it out of submission to being killed and seeking reward, and this is permissible for everyone who is targeted for killing, that he submit and yield. Likewise did ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him) act, and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafiʿi. There is also a third opinion: that what is meant is: if you initiate killing me, I shall not initiate killing you. The sound one of the two [last-mentioned] opinions is the latter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I wish that you would bear my sin and your sin and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is: that you would return bearing the sin of my killing and the sins of yours that preceded it, for Qabil was a bad man. It was also said: he was a disbeliever. And it was said: he is one of the two whom Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in "Ha Mim al-Sajda" (Surah Fussilat): ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Our Lord, show us the ones who misled us from the jinn and mankind."﴾ The one from the jinn is Iblis, and the one from mankind is Qabil. Mujahid said: the meaning of His saying ﴿that you would bear my sin and your sin﴾ is: that you would return bearing the sin of my killing and the sin of your disobedience for which your offering was not accepted, or the sin of your envy of me. This is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Kaysan said: he only said that as a figure of speech, meaning: if I were to kill, the sin would be upon me, and if you were to kill, the sin would be upon you. So I will not kill until you kill, and you will bear both sins, so both sins will be upon you. If someone says: how did he say, "I wish that you would bear my sin and your sin," when the wish to kill or to disobey is not permissible? They answered this in several ways. First: they said: this is not a true wish, but when he knew that he would certainly be killed by him, and he prepared himself to submit, seeking reward, it is as if he wished for his killing figuratively, though he did not wish it in reality. It was also said its meaning is: I wish that you would bear the punishment for my killing and the punishment for your killing, so the wish is in accordance with the judgment of Allah, exalted is He, concerning it, and it is not a wish for the killing itself, but for what the killing necessitates of sin and punishment. And there is a third view: its meaning is: I wish that you would bear my sin and your sin; as if he was restraining him from killing, and he wanted him to abandon killing, so that he would not bear the sin.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 30:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So his soul made him consider the killing of his brother acceptable﴾. Mujahid said: "So his soul encouraged him to it." Qatadah said: "His soul made it appealing to him." It was also said: "It made it easy for him, and his soul submitted to him." From this comes the saying: "A gazelle which the roots of the tree obeyed (ṭāʿat)," meaning: they yielded to her eating of them.

﴿So he killed him, and became one of the losers﴾, meaning: by killing him he lost both this world and the Hereafter. As for this world: he angered his parents and was left without a brother. As for the Hereafter: he angered his Lord and deserved the Fire.

The story of his killing him is that when he wanted to kill him, he did not know how to kill him. Iblis came with a stone and said: "Smash his head with it." In one report, he struck him with that stone while he was submitting to him, and crushed his head. In another report: he ambushed him in his sleep and crushed his head, and so he killed him, and the earth drank his blood. When he came to Adam, Adam said to him: "Where is Habil?" He said: "Have you made me a guardian over him? I do not know!" Adam said to him: "Indeed the earth cries out to me with his blood." Then he cursed the earth which had drunk his blood, so the earth has not drunk blood since then until the Day of Resurrection. Adam wept over him greatly, and he composed, saying:

(The lands have changed, and whoever is upon them,
and the face of the earth is dusty and ugly.)

(Every thing of color and taste has changed,
and the brightness of the beautiful face has diminished.)

This was the first killing that took place among the children of Adam. And in the report: "No man is killed until the Day of Resurrection except that the son of Adam bears a share of it, for he was the first to establish killing."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth﴾. It is related in the narratives (al-qasas) that when Qabil killed [Habil], he returned to him, took him, placed him in a bag, and carried him on his shoulder for forty days. Ibn 'Abbas said: a full year. Mujahid said: a hundred years, until he stank on his shoulder, and he did not know how to conceal him. Then Allah sent two crows, which fought, and one of them killed the other. Then the one that had killed scratched the earth to bury the second. It was also said: it was an angel in the form of a crow ﴿scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the shame of his brother﴾, that is, the corpse of his brother. It was also said: the nakedness (awrah) of his brother, because he had stripped him of his garments.

﴿He said: Woe is me!﴾ This is a word of calling for destruction. ﴿Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the shame of my brother?﴾ That is, am I too weak to be like it? ﴿So he became of those who regret.﴾ If someone says: Was his regret over the killing a repentance from him?

It is said: he did not regret the killing; rather its meaning is that he became one of those who regret having carried him on his shoulder and wandering about with him, because of the fatigue that befell him in that. It was also said: he regretted only because killing him brought little benefit, for it angered his parents and he gained nothing from killing him, so he regretted that, not that he regretted the killing itself. In the narrative it is also related that after he killed him, he became estranged from people, and whenever he met a person he thought that he was coming to kill him, so he fled from him; and he remained like this always, until some of his own sons killed him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Because of that﴾, meaning: because of the treachery of that, ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land﴾. Al-Hasan recited: "aw fasadin fi al-ard" (or corruption in the land). Its interpretation: "without a soul," and "without having done corruption in the land." The well-known reading is "aw fasadin fi al-ard," and its interpretation: "without a soul" and "without corruption in the land," such as disbelief, or fornication, and the like, which makes killing him permissible, according to what he said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, or fornication after marriage, or killing a soul without a soul."

﴿It is as if he had killed all mankind﴾. Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is: whoever kills a soul without a soul, it is as if he has destroyed his own soul, as if he had killed all mankind; (he has destroyed his own soul). ﴿And whoever saves it, it is as if he had saved all mankind﴾, meaning: whoever refrains from killing one of mankind, it is as if he had saved all mankind. Qatadah said: its meaning is that whoever kills a soul, it is as if he had killed all mankind in sin, and whoever saves it, meaning abstains and refrains from killing it, it is as if he had saved all mankind in reward. It was also said: its meaning is: whoever kills a soul, it is as if he had killed all mankind, in the sense that all people are his adversaries in it; and whoever saves it, it is as if he had saved all mankind, in the sense that they thank him and praise him for pardoning or for refraining from killing.

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then indeed many of them after that are, in the land, transgressors﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth [in] corruption is only that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be exiled from the land.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The verse was revealed concerning a people among the polytheists who had a covenant (ʿahd) with the Prophet. They broke the covenant and spread corruption upon the earth.

Anas said: "The verse was revealed concerning a group from ʿUrayna. They came to the Prophet with yellowed faces and swollen bellies, so the Messenger of Allah sent them to the camels of the charity (ṣadaqa), that they might drink from their urine and their milk. They did so, and when they recovered, they killed the herdsman and drove off the camels. The Messenger of Allah sent [men] in pursuit of them, and they were overtaken and brought to the Prophet. He had some of them killed, and some of them had their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, and some of them had their eyes branded with hot iron, and he left them in al-Ḥarra until they died." And concerning them the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾.

It was said: its meaning is that they wage war against the friends of Allah. It was also said: this is a sound usage in Arabic, for whoever disobeys another has in effect waged war against him. Thus, when these people disobey Allah and His Messenger, it is as if they have waged war against Allah and His Messenger. All who disobey, highwaymen (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq), and others are included among them.

As for His saying: ﴿that they be killed or crucified or have their hands cut off﴾, the scholars differed over whether it is in sequence (tartīb) or by choice (takhyīr). Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration, and this is the view of al-Ḥasan, Qatada, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, and Mujahid, said: it is by choice, so the imam chooses among these punishments.

The second view, which is the second narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, and which Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd also held, is that it is in sequence: if they kill, they are killed and crucified; if they take property, their hands and feet are cut off from opposite sides; if they combine taking property and killing, they are cut off and killed; if they terrorize the road without taking property or killing, they are exiled from the land.

Then they differed over exile (nafy). Al-Zuhri said: the imam pursues him in every town where he is caught, and he is exiled from it; likewise, in every town where he is mentioned, he is pursued and exiled from it. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: he is exiled from all the lands of Islam. The people of Kufa said: exile from the land is imprisonment (ḥabs), and imprisonment is a form of exile from the land. A poet, describing imprisoned people, said:

(We went out from the world while we were of its people... so we are neither among the living in it nor among the dead.)

(When the jailer comes to us one day for some need, we are amazed and say: this one has come from the world.)

﴿That is for them a disgrace in this world﴾, i.e., exposure (faḍīḥa) and punishment (nakāl); ﴿and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾

Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is, "except for those who have embraced Islam," because he took the first verse as referring to the polytheists. It was also said: it refers to repentance in its literal sense, so that if highwaymen (qutta' al-tariq) repent before they are captured, the imam grants them safe conduct. This is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), for he granted safe conduct to Haritha ibn Badr when he had committed highway robbery and then repented before he came under his power. It was also said: repentance benefits only with respect to the rights of Allah (ta'ala), whereas the rights of men, such as retaliation (qawd) and property, are not dropped by repentance. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

And His saying ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ is addressed to the rulers (a'imma), meaning: before you gain power over them. ﴿Then know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him﴾. Al-wasilah: nearness (al-qurbah). It was also said: it is the meaning of what came in the report: "Al-wasilah is a rank in Paradise, above which there is no rank." Zayd ibn Aslam said: He meant by it, "Make yourselves beloved to Allah, exalted is He," so al-wasilah carries the meaning of love (al-mahabbah). ﴿And strive in His cause that you may be successful﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—even if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves therewith from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection—it would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ That is: even if they were to ransom themselves with it from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. ﴿It would not be accepted from them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

In a report it is said: "Allah, may He be exalted, will say to the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection: If you had the whole earth filled with gold, would you ransom yourself with it today? He will say: Yes, my Lord. Then Allah, may He be exalted, will say: You were asked for something easier than this."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not be able to come out of it, and theirs is a lasting punishment.﴾ If it is asked: since they will not be coming out of it, how can they wish to come out? It is said: they wish for it out of ignorance, thinking that they will come out.

And it is said: they long for it, so this "wish" carries the sense of longing (tamanni), and it is not a true wish (iradah) in its literal sense.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 38:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "cut off their right hands" (aymanahuma), and this is the meaning of the well-known recitation. If someone says: how does He say ﴿their hands﴾ (aydiyahuma) when the mentioned persons are two, and why does He not say "their two hands" (yadayhuma)? It is said: He did not intend a single male thief or a single female thief; rather He mentioned the category, and therefore He mentioned the hands (al-aydi). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: every body part that is singular in a human being, when two of them are mentioned, is put in the plural. The Exalted says: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ (faqad sagha qulubukuma), and the Arabs say: "I filled their backs and their bellies with blows," though each person has one back and one belly; likewise the right hand of a human being is one, so it is put in the plural when dualized.

If it is said: here He commands the cutting of the instrument of theft, but in the case of adultery He did not command the cutting of the instrument of adultery; what is the wisdom in this? It is said: both are established by the Shari'ah, and their meaning is not rationally discernible. It is also said: the wisdom in it is that whoever cuts off the male organ cuts off offspring, and this is not the case with cutting off the hand; or, because when the hand is cut off and the person is deterred from theft, the left hand remains for him as a substitute for the right; whereas when the male organ is cut off and the deterrence is achieved, no substitute for the male organ remains for him. Therefore the two differ. ﴿A recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah﴾. Al-Nakal (exemplary punishment): every punishment that prevents a person from doing that for which he was punished. ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾; its meaning: capable of punishing the creatures, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He has made obligatory of punishment.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: I used to recite this verse while a Bedouin was beside me, and I recited: "an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." The Bedouin said: "Whose speech is this?" I said: "The speech of Allah." The Bedouin said: "This is not the speech of Allah."

So I became alert and recited ﴿an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾. The Bedouin said: "This is the speech of Allah." Then I asked him about that, and he said: "Allah does not mention a punishment for the servant and then say 'and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful'; rather, what befits the mention of punishment is 'the Mighty, the Wise.'"

Almost all of the passage is commentary, and the Qur'anic quotations are marked with ﴿ ﴾ as required.

God's words, "But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed God will turn to him in forgiveness; indeed God is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (﴿فَمن تَابَ من بعد ظلمه وَأصْلح فَإِن الله يَتُوب عَلَيْهِ إِن الله غَفُور رَحِيم﴾).

Mujahid said: The cutting off of the thief's hand is his repentance; once the hand is cut off, repentance has been achieved. The sound view, however, is that the cutting is a punishment for the crime, as God said: ﴿a recompense for what they earned﴾ (﴿جَزَاء بِمَا كسبا﴾). Therefore repentance is necessary after it, and his repentance is remorse for what has passed and resolve to abandon it in the future.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not know that God—to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ The address is to the Messenger, and what is meant by it is everyone. It was also said: its meaning is, "Do you not know, O human being?" In that case it is an address to every single person among mankind. ﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He punishes whom He wills for minor sins, and forgives whom He wills for major sins. Others said: "He punishes whom He wills" refers to one who dies persisting (in sin), and "forgives whom He wills" refers to one who dies repentant. ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on Surah 5, verse 41:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾. That is, let not their hastening into disbelief grieve you. If it is asked: how could their disbelief not grieve him, when a person grieves over another's disbelief and sin out of compassion for the religion? It is answered: its meaning is, let not the conduct of those who hasten into disbelief grieve you, in the sense that their conduct does not harm you.

﴿Among those who say with their mouths, "We believe," but whose hearts have not believed﴾: this means the hypocrites.

﴿And among those who are Jews, listeners to falsehood﴾: this means the Jews. ﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾ means: they are listeners to falsehood, that is, they are sayers of falsehood, like the worshipper's saying, "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning: God accepts whoever praises Him. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, they listen for the sake of falsehood, for they were ﴿...their hearts...﴾ [a copying fault in the source text] ... ﴿listeners to falsehood, listeners to other people who have not come to you, who distort words after their places. They say, "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware." And whoever God desires to test...﴾ They listen from the Messenger, then go out and lie. ﴿Listeners to other people who have not come to you﴾: that is, spies for other people who have not come to you, namely the people of Khaybar. It describes the hypocrites and the Jews: the hypocrites were spies for the Jews, and the Jews were spies for the people of Khaybar. Sufyan was asked: "Is there any mention of the spy in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes," and recited this verse.

﴿They distort words after their places﴾: that is, after God had placed them in their places. Their distortion of the words is their concealing of the verse of stoning.

﴿And they say, "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware."﴾

The occasion of revelation of this verse [this] is that two Jews from among the Jewish nobles committed adultery. They disliked stoning them, so they said: "Let us send to Muhammad and ask him. If he rules for flogging and tahmim (blackening of the face), we will adopt it; but if he rules otherwise, we will not adopt it." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿If you are given this﴾, meaning what they agreed upon of flogging and tahmim, ﴿take it; but if you are not given it, beware﴾, that is: if he rules for stoning, do not adopt it. It is also said: this was among the Jews of Khaybar, who sent to the Jews of Medina so that they might ask him; they asked the Messenger of God, and he ruled for stoning. The completion of the story is: "He (peace be upon him) summoned Ibn Suriya al-A'war and said: I adjure you by God who sent down the Torah to Moses, what is the punishment for adultery in your book?" He said: "As for you, if you adjure me by God, then the punishment for adultery in our book is stoning, but adultery has become common among our nobles; so when a noble among us committed it, we left him, and when a commoner committed it, we stoned him. Then we agreed upon a matter in which noble and commoner are equal, which is flogging and tahmim." He said: "I am most entitled to revive a sunnah they have caused to die," and he summoned the two Jews who had committed adultery and ordered their stoning. The hadith is in Sahih Muslim.

There is another view concerning the verse: that it is about killing. The story in this regard is that the Banu al-Nadir had a right to kill from the Banu Qurayzah, and whenever a Qurayzi killed, he would ask Muhammad; if he ruled for diyah (blood money), they would accept it, and if he ruled otherwise, they would beware of him. So they asked him, and he ruled for qawd (retaliation in kind). This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware﴾. The first view is more sound.

﴿And whoever God desires to test﴾: al-Suddi said: his misguidance; al-Hasan said: his punishment; al-Zajjaj said: his disgrace. ﴿Then you cannot avail him anything against God﴾: that is, you will not be able to prevent the command of God concerning him.
