His words: ﴿testimony among you﴾ are read in the irregular readings as "shahadatu baynikum" (with the verb reading), and al-A'raj read "shahadatun baynakum" with the nominative and tanwin. The well-known reading is "shahadatu baynikum." ﴿When death approaches one of you, at the time of bequest, two just men from among you﴾: "two" is mentioned in the nominative because it is the predicate of the subject. The meaning of this statement is: the testimony among you concerning the bequest at the time of death is two just men from among you.

﴿Or two others from outside your group﴾: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the view of Shurayh, al-Nakha'i, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and a group, said: its meaning is from outside the people of your religion, that is, from among the dhimmis (protected non-Muslims). Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri said: its meaning is: from outside your tribe.

﴿If you travel in the land﴾, that is, you journey, ﴿and a calamity of death befalls you, you shall detain the two after the prayer﴾. Most scholars hold that it refers to the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr). (Al-Hasan said: after the noon prayer. The first view is more correct.) It was specified for the afternoon prayer because the time of 'Asr is a time of great honour (mu'azzam muhtaram) among all the followers of religions, and people after 'Asr are gathered together in the markets and mosques. What is meant is: detaining the two swearers after 'Asr.

﴿They will swear by Allah, if you doubt: "We will not sell it for any price, even if it were a relative, and we will not conceal the testimony of Allah; indeed we would then be among the sinners."﴾ That is: if doubt arises in you regarding the statement of the swearers or the witnesses who swear that we say only the truth even if it be against a relative. ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾. He said "the testimony of Allah" because testimony is by the command of Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 107:

﴿And if it becomes known that the two had incurred sin﴾ meaning: if it is discovered and their treachery is made apparent, ﴿then two others shall take their place from among those who have a claim against them, the first two﴾. This verse is read in three ways. The first: "min al-ladhina istahaqqa 'alayhimu al-awliyan" (from among those against whom the claim was established, the two nearest). Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "min al-ladhina istahaqqa" with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', ﴿'alayhimu al-awliyan﴾. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, and Hamzah read "min al-ladhina istuhiqqa" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', ﴿'alayhimu al-awwalin﴾.

As for the meaning of the first reading, His words ﴿istahaqqa 'alayhim﴾ mean: "istahaqqa fihim" (it was established concerning them) or "istahaqqa min-hum" (it was established from them), like His words ﴿and I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ meaning "upon the trunks of palm trees". This refers to those against whom the treachery was committed, namely the heirs of the deceased. And ﴿al-awliyan﴾ is the dual of "al-uwla", and "al-uwla" means "the closer"; its meaning is: if treachery of the two swearers is discovered, then the two nearest of the heirs of the deceased shall stand up and swear. As for His words ﴿from among those against whom it was established﴾, meaning a right was established and became obligatory upon them, its meaning and the meaning of the first reading are the same.

As for the third reading, ﴿min al-ladhina istuhiqqa 'alayhim al-awwalin﴾, it is a substitute for His words ﴿from among those who﴾ or for the pronoun hidden under His words ﴿'alayhim﴾; so it refers also to the heirs of the deceased, and the meaning is as we have explained.

Then He explained the manner of their oath, saying: ﴿They shall swear by God: "Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed; otherwise we would indeed be among the wrongdoers."﴾

ﷺ

﴿That is more likely that they will give testimony in its proper form, or fear that oaths will be reversed after their oaths.﴾ Meaning: that is closer and more fitting for you to render the testimony in its proper form. ﴿Or fear that oaths will be reversed after their oaths.﴾ Meaning: or if they fear that the oath will be returned after their oath to the claimants, so they do not swear falsely, out of fear that the oath will be returned upon them, and their oath would then be the one that stands.

﴿And fear Allah and listen. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ Al-Nakha'i and Shurayh said: the verse is abrogated (mansukhah), and His saying: ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾ — the testimony of the People of the Dhimma (ahl al-dhimma) was accepted in bequests, then it was abrogated. Some of them permitted the testimony of the People of the Dhimma in bequests specifically, namely those among them who do not hold that the verse has been abrogated. Al-Hasan said: the verse is muhkamah (not abrogated), and His saying: "or two others from among other than you" has been interpreted as referring to other than your tribe, as we have explained.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 109:

His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers and say, "What was the response you received?" They will say, "We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ If someone asks: how can they say "We have no knowledge," when they already know what response they gave? It is said: Hell will emit a roar that bewilders their minds (ʿuqūl), so that from the intensity of terror they say, "We have no knowledge." Then Allah, may He be exalted, will restore their minds to them, and they will inform Him of the answer. It is also said: the meaning is, "We have no knowledge except what You Yourself know better than us," or, "except what You have taught us." It is also said: the meaning is, "We have no knowledge of the wisdom in Your asking us about a matter of which You are more knowing than we are." It is also said: the meaning is, "We have no knowledge of the final outcome of their affairs, nor of what they innovated after us, nor on what their affair was concluded."

Two things indicate this. The first is from the verse, His saying ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾. The second is what is related in an authentic report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "A group of my companions will be driven to the left (on the Day of Resurrection), and I will say, 'O Lord, my companions, my companions!' Allah, Blessed and Exalted, will say, 'You do not know what they innovated after you. Indeed, they have continued to turn back on their heels since you parted from them.' Then I will say what the righteous servant said: ﴿And I was a witness over them while I remained among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things.﴾"

The Most High's saying: ﴿When Allah said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother."﴾ He commanded him to be grateful for the blessing, then enumerated a blessing for him, saying: ﴿When I supported you with the Holy Spirit, you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; and when I taught you the Book and wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel.﴾ We have already discussed this.

﴿And when you shaped from clay [something] like the form of a bird by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission.﴾ We have explained its manner earlier. ﴿And you healed the blind and the leper by My permission. And when you brought out the dead by My permission. And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you when you came to them with clear proofs, and those of them who disbelieved said, "This is nothing but evident magic."﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 111:

The Exalted said: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), saying: Believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾. This "wahy" (inspiration) is in the sense of ilham (inspiration of the heart), or in the sense of amr (command), meaning: I inspired them and commanded them. Al-'Ajjaj said:

(All praise is due to God, by whom the sky was held up and became still,
(He) "inspired" it to settle, so it settled.)

Meaning: He commanded it to settle.

﴿They said: We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of al-Hawariyyun (the disciples).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 112:

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, is your Lord able to send down to us a table spread with food from the heaven?"﴾ Al-Kisa'i recited: "Is your Lord able" (هَل يَسْتَطِيع), with the ta' (التاء) read as a feminine prefix, and "your Lord" (رَبك) with a fatha on the ba' (الْبَاء). This is also the reading of 'Ali, Mu'adh and 'A'isha. 'A'isha used to swear that the disciples were too knowledgeable about Allah to say: "Is your Lord able?"

This reading has two meanings. The first: the intended meaning is "Do you ask your Lord?" The second: "Would your Lord's obedience be shown by answering your request?" As for the well-known reading, there are several views on its meaning:

The first view is that its meaning is: "Would your Lord act?" Al-Farra' said: a man says to another, "Are you able (hal tastati'u) to do such-and-such?", meaning: "Will you do such-and-such?"

The second meaning is that it means: "Would your Lord obey you (yuti'u)?" Here istata'a is used in the sense of ata'a (to obey), as in the expression istajaba, meaning ajaba (to answer). So the meaning is: "Would your Lord obey you by answering your request?" In the traditions: "Whoever obeys Allah, Allah obeys him," meaning: He answers his supplication.

It has also been said that the disciples said this before their knowledge was firmly established, and that they meant by it "power." Had their knowledge been firm, they would not have said that. The correct view is one of the first two opinions, because "istita'a" is generally not attributed to Allah; rather, He is described with "qudra" (power), whereas "istita'a" pertains to the servant.

As for His saying: ﴿that He send down to us a table from the heaven﴾: know that "al-ma'ida" (the table) is the name for that upon which food is placed; if there is no food on it, it is not called a ma'ida. They differed about its derivation. Some said it is from "al-maid," meaning giving, and from this they said of the Commander of the Faithful: "al-mumtad," meaning the one whose gift is sought. Accordingly, it was called a ma'ida because it gives food to those upon it.

It has also been said that it is from "al-maid" meaning movement; accordingly, it was called a ma'ida because it moves with the food upon it.

﴿He said: "Fear Allah, if you are believers."﴾ He forbade them from demanding signs after faith. It was also said that he meant: be content with the food of the earth instead of the food of heaven.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it"﴾, meaning eating for blessing (tabarruk, seeking blessing), not eating out of need. ﴿And that our hearts may be reassured﴾, meaning that their faith may increase. This is like His saying: ﴿But that my heart may be at rest﴾ and "we know that you have spoken the truth to us," meaning that we may increase in faith through your truthfulness.

In some exegetical reports, when they asked him to request the al-ma'idah (the table spread with food), ʿIsa, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, had commanded them to fast thirty days. He said to them: "Fast thirty days; when you break your fast, you will not ask God for anything except that He gives it to you." They did so, and when the table was given to them, they recognized his truthfulness. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and we know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be among its witnesses﴾.

The Quranic verse: "Jesus, son of Mary, said: O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table (ma'idah) from heaven, to be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us." Some say that when he wished to ask for the table, he performed ghusl (full ritual bath), prayed two units of prayer (rak'atayn), lowered his head, cast his gaze down, and wept. Then he said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, to be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us." The word "festival" ('id) here means a day of joy for them. ﴿And a sign from You, and provide for us, and You are the best of providers.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 5, verse 115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God said, "Indeed I will send it down to you. Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment I have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds."﴾ That is, a kind of punishment with which I have not punished anyone. It is also said that this punishment was that He transformed them into swine, as we will explain in the narrative.

Then they differed. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: the table (al-ma'idah) was never sent down at all. When God threatened punishment for their disbelief after the table's descent, they feared that some of them would disbelieve, so they asked to be excused from the table's descent. According to this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed I will send it down to you﴾ is: if you ask. However, they asked to be excused, so it was not sent down. The sound view, which the majority hold, is that it was sent down, because God, may He be exalted, does not promise something and then fail to fulfil it, and He has said: ﴿Indeed I will send it down to you﴾.

The narrative concerning this is that when Jesus asked for the table, a red tray (sufrah) descended from the sky between two clouds, which they could see. It was spread before them, and it was covered. Jesus stood up to it and lifted its covering, and on it were seven loaves and seven fishes. In another report: on it were five loaves and a roasted fish, with no scales or bones as are found in the fish of the earth, and around it were all kinds of herbs except for the leeks (al-kurrat), and at its head was salt and at its tail was vinegar, and on it were five pomegranates and dates. It is also said that the loaves were of rice bread. ʿAṭiyyah said: on it was a fish that had the taste of all the earth. It is also said: on it was fruit from the fruits of Paradise. In some reports, Jesus was asked: "Is this from the food of Paradise?" He said: "Neither from the food of Paradise nor from the food of the earth; it is food which God, may He be exalted, created for you."

In the narrative: when this table descended, Jesus invited the poor, the chronically ill, and the needy to eat from it. It would descend upon them for forty days, and each day four thousand or five thousand people would eat from it, and they would eat and nothing would diminish from it. Then it would ascend and descend again, thus every day, until they betrayed it, and they were transformed into apes and swine, and the table was lifted up.

Then they differed about what that betrayal was. ʿAmmar ibn Yasir reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The table was sent down upon them, and on it was bread and meat, and they were commanded not to store any of it for the next day. They stored it and betrayed, so they awoke as apes and swine." In another report: "They awoke as swine." It is also said that their betrayal was that the Jews said to them: "Jesus has bewitched you with the table," and there was no table; so they doubted him, and they were transformed into swine. It is also said that their betrayal was that at the beginning the rich and the poor used to eat from it together; so God, may He be exalted, commanded them to invite the poor to it instead of the rich; He tested them, and the rich ate and disobeyed, so they awoke as swine. ﴿Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?" He said, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your self."﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 116:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary..."﴾. Scholars differed about when this statement will take place. Al-Suddi said: Allah, exalted is He, said that when He raised him to the heaven, because His saying "idh" (when) is for the past. The correct view, however, is that it will occur on the Day of Resurrection. The Resurrection, although it has not yet happened, is in the knowledge of Allah; since it is certain to occur, it is as though it has already occurred. Thus His saying ﴿And when Allah says﴾ is valid. It was also said that "idha" (when) here carries the meaning of "idh" (when), and such usage is permissible. A poet said:

(The God did not reward him with it when He rewarded / the gardens of Eden in the highest heavens)

He means: "when He rewarded." ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ It was said: this is a question of rebuke, and it is directed at his people. The wisdom in asking him about it was so that his people would hear his denial, because they used to claim that Jesus had commanded them to take him as a god. If someone says: they did not take his mother as a god, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah﴾? It is answered: when He, Mighty and Majestic, wished to mention Jesus together with his mother, He said "two gods" (ilahayn). This is like what is said when mentioning Abu Bakr and Umar together: "Umarayn," and they said: "This is the Sunnah of the two Umars." And the sun and the moon are called "qamarان" (the two moons). Al-Farazdaq said:

(For us are its two moons, and the stars rising)

He means: the sun and the moon. It was also said: Jesus was a part of Mary, so when they took him as a god, it was as though they had taken his mother as a god; hence He said: ﴿two gods besides Allah﴾. ﴿He said: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul."﴾ He first occupied himself with praising Him and declaring Him free of imperfection, and he attributed to Him holiness and purity. ﴿You know what is in my soul and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the "nafs" (soul) of a prophet means his whole self and reality, so the meaning is: You know the reality of my affair, and I do not know the reality of Your affair. It was also said: the meaning is: You know what is in my unseen and I do not know what is in Your unseen, and this is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed You are the Knower of the unseen⁠﴾, and this is the meaning of the first view.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 117:

﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them. But when You took me up (tawaffaytani), You were the Watcher over them, and You are, over all things, Witness.﴾

Meaning: "raftani" (You raised me up).

﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾, and we have already explained the meaning of tawaffi (taking up, causing to die) earlier.

﴿And You are, over all things, Witness.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ If someone says: How did He request forgiveness for them when they are disbelievers? And how did He say, "And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise," when this is not fitting for a request for forgiveness?

It is said: As for the first, the meaning of His saying, "And if You forgive them," is: after faith. This only holds according to the view of al-Suddi, because faith does not benefit on the Day of Resurrection. The sound one of the two views is the last of them. Some of them said: this refers to two groups among them. So His saying, "If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants," means: whoever of them disbelieved. "And if You forgive them" means: whoever of them believed.

The scholars of meanings among the grammarians said: this is not in the form of requesting forgiveness, but rather it is a submission of the matter to Him and entrusting it to His will. Do you not see that He says, "indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise"? Had it been in the form of requesting forgiveness, He would have said, "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful."

As for the second question: know that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." Ibn Shanbudh used to recite it that way for a period in Baghdad; he was prohibited from it, and there is a story concerning this. It is also said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it, and the intended sense of the verse is: "If You forgive them, indeed they are Your servants, and if You punish them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise." It is also said: its meaning is: if You forgive them, nothing diminishes from Your might (ʿizz) and nothing departs from Your wisdom (hikmah). The wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, and the breadth of His mercy include forgiving the disbelievers, but He has informed that He will not forgive them, and He does not break His report. Whoever says that it is a submission of the matter and not in the form of requesting forgiveness, the arrangement of the verse holds together according to his view, as we have explained.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 5, verses 119–120:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah said: "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾ It is read "yawm" (day) with a nominative (raf') vowel, as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), and it is read "yawm" with an accusative (nasb) vowel, as if he intended "fi yawm" (on a day), so the preposition "fi" was omitted and "yawm" was put in the accusative.

If someone says: How can the truthful benefit from their truthfulness on the Day of Resurrection, when it is not an abode of benefit? It is said: Its meaning is that the truthful benefit from their truthfulness in this world, not from their truthfulness on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: Their benefit from truthfulness on the Day of Resurrection is that, had they lied, their limbs would have spoken and they would have been disgraced; but when they are truthful, they are not disgraced. (﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph.﴾ To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.) And Allah knows best what is correct.
